rv.q: Otherwise, the production marches rather dully to a foreshadowed conclusion, navigating O'Neill's endlessly indulgent soliloquies along the way.

At one point, following a tip he received during a stint in jail, he turns up at the office of Industrial Workers of the World, thinking he can use his sheer brawn and fearlessness to make a difference, and is utterly humiliated—though as anyone familiar with the play knows, worse lies ahead.

Through stunning period design, brutally efficient staging, and memorable performances, O'Reilly and company show how this 1922 'comedy of ancient and modern life' is, in fact, an ongoing tragedy in 2026.
How well does O'Reilly bring O'Neill's angry (gorilla-like?) opus to the stage? Moderately well.
For all this expertise and some solid acting, a preview performance the other evening was not as striking as might be expected.

Ciarán O'Reilly's stylish revival benefits from an evocative set and lighting design that makes the most of the Irish Rep's cramped stage as well as a star-making turn by Jon Beavers ( Paradise ) in the title role.

cn.t: Jon Beavers delivers a strong performance in this timely revival of O'Neill's expressionist class drama, though critics split on whether the century-old play transcends its two-note protagonist.
